metadata.title: How does PISA assess science literacy?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA in Focus brief describes the PISA 2015 science assessment design and delivery mode rather than conducting an original student-level statistical analysis. It reports that about 540 000 15-year-old students participated across more than 70 economies, with the science test administered primarily on computers (with some countries/economies having a paper option). Because no analytic dataset, weighting variables, or variance estimation approach are specified, the manuscript does not provide information on whether complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or replicate weights were applied. For any secondary analysis using PISA microdata, analysts should use the official PISA sampling weights and replicate-weight procedures provided in the PISA database documentation to account for the complex two-stage sampling and school clustering.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is a descriptive policy/assessment overview of how PISA measures science literacy (skills and item formats), not an empirical analysis predicting an achievement outcome from microdata. As a result, plausible values (PV-based achievement scores) and a missing-data handling strategy are not part of the reported methodology. The brief therefore does not specify PV computation/combination or missing-data procedures, which would only be relevant in an original statistical modeling study using PISA microdata.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The brief reports participation in PISA 2015 science by about 540 000 15-year-old students across more than 70 economies, but it does not describe any analytic subsample restrictions (e.g., grade bands, school types, or task/module completion filters). It also does not specify whether the reported figures correspond to the full PISA 2015 science sample or to a particular subset (e.g., computer-based only).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus brief explains how PISA 2015 assesses science literacy among 15-year-olds, emphasizing competencies rather than factual recall. Science literacy is defined as the ability to engage with science-related issues as a reflective citizen, operationalized through three skills: explaining phenomena scientifically, evaluating and designing scientific enquiry, and interpreting data and evidence scientifically. The brief highlights a major assessment change between PISA 2006 and PISA 2015: the move from pencil-and-paper to computer-based delivery for most participating students, enabling more extensive and nuanced measurement (including simulation-based enquiry tasks). It reports that about 540 000 students in more than 70 economies participated, with new participating economies including Beijing-Shanghai-Jiangsu-Guangdong (reported as B-S-J-G/China), Algeria, the Dominican Republic, Kosovo, and Lebanon. No model-based results, performance metrics, or causal/predictive estimates are presented because the document is not an empirical ML study.
